deep.reconstruction:
Context (end of the previous page, §§378–385). For a prime d, Euler has shown that the cubic residues x^3 mod d (1 ≤ x < d) are either all distinct or coincide in triples. Triples can occur only when 3 | d−1, i.e. for d = 6q+1. The triple case certainly occurs when d divides a^2+ab+b^2, equivalently a form a^2+3b^2. In §385 he notes that the prime divisors of x^2+3y^2 lie in the classes 12q+1 and 12q+7, which merge into 6q+1.

Top of p.48. Hence, conversely, one may conjecture that every prime 6q+1 has 'that property', namely that cubes repeat in triples (equivalently, that it divides some a^2+3b^2). Euler says a full proof is still lacking.

§386 (granting this). Take the cubes 1^3, 2^3, …, (6q)^3 = 216q^3 modulo a prime d.
- If d = 6q+1, the residues coincide in threes. So there are exactly 2q distinct cubic residues and 4q cubic non-residues.
- If d is not of that form, all 6q residues are distinct and there are no non-residues.

Modern form: for p ≡ 1 (mod 3), x ↦ x^3 on (Z/p)^* is 3-to-1, with image of size (p−1)/3. For p ≡ 2 (mod 3) it is a bijection.

§387. Only primes 6q+1 need study; there #non-residues = 2·#residues. Tables are given for d = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43:
- 7: residues {1, 6}.
- 13: residues {1, 5, 8, 12}.
- 19: residues {1, 7, 8, 11, 12, 18}.
- 31: residues {±1, ±2, ±4, ±8, ±16}.
- 37: residues {±1, ±6, ±8, ±10, ±11, ±14}.
- 43: residues {±1, ±2, ±4, ±8, ±11, ±16, ±21}.

In each case the non-residues are listed in two rows, k and d−k. This reflects that −1 = (−1)^3 is a residue, so the residue and non-residue sets are closed under negation.

§388. The residues contain:
- all cubes below d;
- their complements d−1 = 6q, d−8 = 6q−7, d−27 = 6q−26, d−64 = 6q−63, …;
- all products of two residues.

Moreover, if mn and m are residues, so is n. In modern terms, the cubic residues form a subgroup of (Z/d)^*.

§389 (proof of the quotient property). Suppose a^3 ≡ mn and b^3 ≡ m. Choose f, g with a = fb − gd, i.e. f ≡ a b^{-1}, which exists since d is prime and d ∤ b (implicit). Then f^3 b^3 ≡ mn ≡ n b^3. So d | b^3 (f^3 − n), hence d | f^3 − n, and n ≡ f^3.

§390. If a ≡ x^3 is a cubic residue mod d = 6q+1, then a^{2q} ≡ x^{6q} ≡ 1 by Fermat. So the residues of the geometric progression 1, a, …, a^{2q} lie among the cubic residues. This is the necessity half of Euler's criterion for cubic residues.

§391 (begins the converse). If d = 6q+1 is prime and d | a^{2q} − 1, then a is a cubic residue. Euler says this is easy when 3 ∤ 2q. The completion is on the next page (my reading): write 2q = 3k ± 1. Then a^{3k±1} ≡ 1 is a residue and a^{3k} is a cube, so by the quotient property a^{±1}, hence a, is a residue. Note that this case can arise only for exponents 2q with 3 ∤ 2q, i.e. p ≢ 1 (mod 9).
errors: §390: the claim that the residues of 1, a, a^2, …, a^{2q} 'coincide with' the cubic residues is an overstatement. They are always a subset of the 2q cubic residues; equality holds only when a has multiplicative order exactly 2q, i.e. generates the subgroup of cubes. Example: a = 1, or a = −1 (order 2), gives only 1 or 2 residues.
§389: the argument tacitly assumes d ∤ b, so that f with fb ≡ a exists and b^3 can be cancelled. This is harmless for nonzero residues.

§386 rests on an admitted unproved hypothesis: that every prime 6q+1 has the triple-coincidence property, equivalently divides some a^2+3b^2. Euler explicitly flags this ('plena demonstratio adhuc desideratur'). The statement is true: the cube map on a cyclic group of order 6q is 3-to-1, or −3 is a QR mod p for p ≡ 1 (mod 3).
All six tables were checked and are numerically correct. No arithmetic slips were found.

results.what: For prime p = 6q+1 there are exactly 2q = (p−1)/3 cubic residues and 4q non-residues. For primes p ≡ 2 (mod 3) every number is a cubic residue.
results.modern_name: Counting cubic residues; the cube map on the cyclic group (Z/p)^* has kernel of size gcd(3, p−1).
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tractatus de numerorum doctrina c.1750, E792; also E262/E449 on power residues), later systematized by Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801).

results.what: Tables of cubic residues and non-residues for p = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43.
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (this treatise); later Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus (1839) gives extensive tables.

results.what: Cubic residues are closed under products and quotients (if mn and m are residues, so is n).
results.modern_name: The cubic residues form a subgroup of (Z/p)^*.

results.what: a is a cubic residue mod p = 6q+1 implies a^{2q} ≡ 1 (mod p). The converse is begun here and proved on the next page in the easy case 3 ∤ 2q.
results.modern_name: Euler's criterion for cubic (power) residues: a is a k-th power residue iff a^{(p−1)/gcd(k, p−1)} ≡ 1.
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262, 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta', 1761; Tractatus c.1750); fully proved via primitive roots by Gauss.

results.what: Conjecture that every prime 6q+1 has the triple-coincidence property, equivalently divides a^2+3b^2 (-3 is a QR mod p).
results.modern_name: Primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3) are represented by x^2+3y^2 / (−3|p) = 1 iff p ≡ 1 (mod 3).

deep.surprise_reason: This is the known content of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. 11 (published 1849 in Opera Postuma). Cubic residue counts, residue tables and the cubic Euler criterion are standard and well attributed to Euler. Nothing goes beyond his published work on power residues.

checkable.sympy: all((pow(a,(p-1)//3,p)==1) == (a in set(pow(x,3,p) for x in range(1,p))) for p in sympy.primerange(7,400) if p%3==1 for a in range(1,p))
checkable.asserts: §§390–391: Euler's criterion, a is a cubic residue mod p=6q+1 iff a^(2q) ≡ 1

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.legendre_symbol(-3 % p, p) == 1 for p in sympy.primerange(7,5000) if p%6==1)
checkable.asserts: The conjectured property at the top of the page: every prime 6q+1 divides some a^2+3b^2

In the 43 table the image has 'non-residua' without a colon; this is cosmetic.
